\subsubsection{Benchmarks}

\paragraph{Which benchmarks still challenge frontier systems?}
\textit{Progress is fastest where evaluation is densest---perceived stagnation often reflects measurement gaps, not capability plateaus.}
Historical progress has concentrated in domains with dense leaderboard coverage---Mathematics \& Reasoning and competitive coding---where scores approach saturation within months of release (Appendix~\ref{app:overtime}).  Agent-intensive domains (tool use, scientific research, long-horizon planning) show sparser measurement histories and substantially more remaining headroom, suggesting that \emph{evaluation infrastructure}, not only capability, gates perceived progress.

Among the \NumIncludedBenchmarks{} benchmarks in our evaluation, roughly one-fifth (\NumSaturatedBenchmarks{}) are effectively saturated ($>$95\% best score), spanning traditionally ``hard'' tasks such as AIME and GPQA Diamond.  The remaining challenge concentrates unevenly: Software Engineering simultaneously hosts solved function-level tasks and unsolved system-level challenges where frontier systems still score below 50\% (Figure~\ref{fig:headroom-by-domain}).  This within-domain heterogeneity---between well-specified, unit-testable problems and open-ended engineering---marks the boundary of current agentic capability.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{\FigHeadroomByDomain}
  \caption{Best system score per benchmark, colored by domain.  Benchmarks are sorted within each domain by best score; shaded area indicates remaining headroom.}
  \label{fig:headroom-by-domain}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{How many benchmarks do we actually need?}
\textit{A single capability axis dominates model-only evaluation; agent scaffolding introduces a structurally distinct second dimension.}
Applying BenchPress-style matrix completion~\cite{papailiopoulos2026benchpress} to our \AppNumSystems{}-system $\times$ \NumIncludedBenchmarks{}-benchmark matrix, a single principal component captures \AppSVDModelOnlyPCOne{}\% of variance under the minimal Terminus-2 scaffold---comparable to the 71\% reported by BenchPress on model-only matrices.  When advanced scaffolds are included, a second orthogonal component emerges (\AppSVDFullPCTwo{}\% additional variance) that cleanly separates scaffolded from unscaffolded systems (Appendix~\ref{app:benchpress}).

\textit{Difficulty and uniqueness are decoupled.}
Greedy forward selection retains only \GreedyBenchmarksBelowSeven{} of \NumIncludedBenchmarks{} benchmarks at the $|\rho|<0.7$ pairwise Spearman independence threshold.  Benchmarks that resist prediction tend to involve open-ended exploration, multi-step tool use, or domain-specific reasoning---capabilities orthogonal to the dominant axis.  Some of the hardest benchmarks are fully predicted by easier ones, while moderate-difficulty tasks provide irreplaceable signal.  This motivates evaluation design that prioritizes \emph{coverage of independent capability axes} over raw difficulty.

\subsubsection{Agent Harness}
\label{sec:agent-harness}

\paragraph{Which matters more: the model or the scaffold?}
\textit{The foundation model is the binding constraint; scaffolding modulates how capability is deployed but does not substitute for capability itself.}
Across all three provider families, upgrading the base model produces \AnthropicModelAgentRatio{}--\OpenAIModelAgentRatio{}$\times$ larger score changes than switching the scaffold (Appendix~\ref{app:within-family}).  When adjusting for baseline difficulty across all \NumModels{} models and \NumAgents{} agents, variance attributable to the model exceeds that of the scaffold by over an order of magnitude.

\paragraph{When does scaffolding help?}
\textit{Scaffolding requires a \emph{competence floor}; above it, two contrasting regimes emerge.}
The base model must be strong enough to absorb the orchestration overhead---planning, tool dispatch, context management---that the scaffold imposes.  Below this floor, agentic wrapping \emph{degrades} results (Table~\ref{tab:agent-lift}).

\begin{table}[t]\small
\centering
\caption{Agent lift over Terminus~2 by model tier.  $\Delta$: mean normalized score change; Positive Lift: fraction of benchmarks where the scaffold strictly improves upon the neutral harness.}
\label{tab:agent-lift}
\begin{tabular*}{\linewidth}{@{\extracolsep{\fill}}llccc@{}}
\toprule
Family & Model (tier) & Base & Agent $\Delta$ & Pos.\ Lift \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{OpenAI + Codex}
  & GPT-5.4 (strong)  & \GPTFiveFourBase & \GPTFiveFourDelta & \GPTFiveFourLift\% \\
  & GPT-5-Mini (mid)   & \GPTMiniBase & \GPTMiniDelta & \GPTMiniLift\% \\
  & GPT-5-Nano (weak)  & \GPTNanoBase & \GPTNanoDelta & \GPTNanoLift\% \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Anthropic + Claude Code}
  & Claude-Opus (strong)  & \ClaudeOpusBase & \ClaudeOpusDelta & \ClaudeOpusLift\% \\
  & Claude-Sonnet (mid)   & \ClaudeSonnetBase & \ClaudeSonnetDelta & \ClaudeSonnetLift\% \\
  & Claude-Haiku (weak)   & \ClaudeHaikuBase & \ClaudeHaikuDelta & \ClaudeHaikuLift\% \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Google + Gemini CLI}
  & Gemini Pro (strong) & \GeminiProBase & \GeminiProDelta & \GeminiProLift\% \\
  & Gemini Flash (mid)  & \GeminiFlashBase & \GeminiFlashDelta & \GeminiFlashLift\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular*}
\end{table}

Above this floor, scaffold design interacts with model strength in two distinct ways:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=1.5em]
  \item \textbf{Capability amplification} (Codex)---gains scale \emph{with} base-model strength, consistent with a scaffold that unlocks latent capabilities the model cannot deploy in single-turn evaluation.
  \item \textbf{Gap closing} (Claude~Code)---gains scale \emph{inversely} with base-model strength, consistent with a scaffold that compensates for weaknesses via retry and decomposition.
\end{itemize}
These two regimes suggest that there is no universally optimal scaffold: strong models need an orchestrator that \emph{expands} their action space, while weaker models need one that \emph{constrains and corrects}.
